Paradoxically, evolutionary adaptation is occurring on both sides: within 70 years, the body size and relative leg length of leading-edge toads have increased (facilitating faster spread), while quolls in invaded areas have evolved toad-aversion behaviors through natural selection within just 13 generations.

Phase separation — the condensation of biomolecules into liquid-like droplets (biomolecular condensates) through weak multivalent interactions — is a newly recognized organizing principle of cell biology. Stress granules, P bodies, nucleoli, heterochromatin domains, and transcriptional enhancer hubs (super-enhancers) are membraneless organelles assembled by phase separation of intrinsically disordered protein regions (IDRs) and RNA. Disease-linked mutations in phase-separating proteins (FUS, TDP-43 in ALS; G3BP1 in stress granule formation) convert dynamic liquid condensates into solid pathological aggregates.

Biodiversity hotspots — 36 regions identified by Conservation International covering just 2.5% of Earth's land area — harbor >50% of the world's plant species and >42% of terrestrial vertebrate species as endemics. The most species-rich hotspot is the Sundaland (Borneo, Sumatra, Java, Philippines), followed by the Tropical Andes and the Mediterranean Basin. All hotspots have lost at least 70% of their original habitat; together they account for ~34% of the habitats of all threatened terrestrial vertebrates while receiving only a small fraction of global conservation funding.

G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) constitute the largest family of membrane receptors in the human genome (~800 members) and mediate responses to photons (rhodopsin), odorants, hormones, neurotransmitters, and drugs. Agonist binding induces conformational change activating heterotrimeric G proteins (Gs, Gi, Gq, G12/13), which regulate adenylate cyclase (cAMP), phospholipase C (IP3/DAG), or ion channels. GPCRs are targets for ~35% of all FDA-approved drugs. Robert Lefkowitz and Brian Kobilka shared the 2012 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for elucidating GPCR structure and signaling mechanisms.

Protein misfolding diseases include Alzheimer's (amyloid-beta plaques and tau tangles), Parkinson's (alpha-synuclein Lewy bodies), Huntington's (polyglutamine aggregates), and type 2 diabetes (IAPP/amylin amyloid in pancreatic islets). Common features include templated self-propagating fibrillar beta-sheet aggregates, prion-like cell-to-cell spreading of aggregate seeds, and failure of cellular proteostasis (chaperones, UPS, autophagy) to clear aggregates. Small molecule chaperones, antisense oligonucleotides (tofersen for SOD1-ALS), and passive immunotherapy targeting amyloid-beta (lecanemab, donanemab) represent current therapeutic strategies.

The tree of life has been radically redrawn by molecular phylogenetics. Based on 16S/18S rRNA sequences, all cellular life falls into three domains: Bacteria, Archaea, and Eukarya. Eukaryotes are nested within Archaea (specifically the Asgard superphylum) in the two-domain model — making the 'tree of life' actually a web where eukaryotes arose by endosymbiosis and gene flow from archaeal and bacterial sources. Phylogenomics (using hundreds of conserved genes simultaneously) has resolved many contested deep branches including the root of the eukaryotic tree and the relationship of the major fungal phyla.

Salamanders of the genus Plethodon (lungless salamanders) respire entirely through their moist skin and mouth lining — they have no lungs. This represents a secondary loss from the tetrapod ancestor; lunglessness evolved once in plethodontids (~455 described species, the largest salamander family) but has not re-evolved. Their high moisture requirements restrict them to cool, humid forest habitats, making them sensitive indicators of forest microclimate; they are among the most abundant vertebrates by biomass in Appalachian forests, playing critical roles in nutrient cycling and soil carbon turnover.

Endocannabinoids (anandamide and 2-arachidonoylglycerol, 2-AG) are lipid signaling molecules produced on-demand from membrane phospholipids in postsynaptic neurons and act as retrograde neurotransmitters — traveling backwards across synapses to activate presynaptic CB1 receptors, suppressing further neurotransmitter release (DSI/DSE: depolarization-induced suppression of inhibition/excitation). The endocannabinoid system regulates synaptic plasticity, pain modulation, appetite, mood, and memory. THC (tetrahydrocannabinol) from Cannabis sativa is a partial agonist of CB1 receptors, mimicking endocannabinoid activity and producing psychoactive effects.

Aging is the progressive functional decline and increased mortality that occurs in most organisms after reproductive maturity. Major theories of aging include: accumulated DNA damage (damaged mitochondrial DNA leading to dysfunctional electron transport), telomere shortening inducing senescence, protein aggregation and proteostasis failure, epigenetic clock drift (measurable methylation changes predicting biological age), and depletion of adult stem cell pools. Interventions extending lifespan in model organisms include caloric restriction, rapamycin (mTOR inhibition), metformin, NAD+ precursors, and germline manipulation in C. elegans.

Calcium imaging uses fluorescent dyes (Fura-2, Fluo-4) or genetically encoded calcium indicators (GECIs, GCaMP series) to measure intracellular calcium dynamics in live cells and tissues. GCaMP6 — an engineered fusion of GFP, calmodulin, and M13 peptide that undergoes fluorescence changes upon Ca2+ binding — can resolve single action potentials in neurons with millisecond precision. Two-photon calcium imaging with GCaMP enables recording of hundreds to thousands of neurons simultaneously in behaving animals, revolutionizing systems neuroscience by revealing population coding of sensory stimuli, decisions, and memories.

The respiratory quotient (RQ) — the ratio of CO2 produced to O2 consumed during cellular respiration — varies with fuel: RQ = 1.0 for carbohydrates (equal moles CO2 and O2), ~0.7 for fats (more C-H bonds requiring more O2), and ~0.8 for proteins. A person burning predominantly fat has RQ near 0.7; an athlete at peak aerobic exercise may reach RQ >1.0 from anaerobic lactate production adding CO2 without extra O2 consumption. RQ measurement guides nutritional assessment and metabolic rate estimation in clinical settings.

The discovery that some RNA molecules function as enzymes (ribozymes) — demonstrated by Thomas Cech for self-splicing Group I introns and Sidney Altman for RNase P in 1989 (shared Nobel Prize in Chemistry) — transformed understanding of life's origins. The RNA world hypothesis proposes that early life was based on self-replicating RNA molecules that both stored genetic information and catalyzed chemical reactions, before the evolution of DNA (more stable) as the information store and proteins (more versatile) as catalysts. The ribosome's peptidyl transferase center being RNA supports a vestige of the RNA world.

Genome size varies enormously across life and does not correlate with organismal complexity (the 'C-value paradox'): the lungfish genome (~133 Gb) is ~43× larger than the human genome (~3 Gb); the Paris japonica plant genome (~149 Gb) is 50× larger than the human genome; Arabidopsis thaliana has a tiny plant genome (~135 Mb). Much genome size variation reflects differences in transposable element content and non-coding DNA rather than gene number — organism function is encoded more in regulatory networks than in gene count.

The human placenta produces human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) immediately after implantation, preventing corpus luteum regression and maintaining progesterone production to sustain early pregnancy. This is the hormone detected by pregnancy tests (immunoassays detecting hCG in urine), which can detect pregnancy as early as 6–10 days after fertilization. Some cancers (choriocarcinoma, testicular germ cell tumors) also produce hCG, making it a useful tumor marker; monitoring hCG decline after treatment verifies complete tumor removal.

The phosphorus cycle lacks a gaseous atmospheric phase (unlike carbon or nitrogen), making weathering of phosphate-containing rocks the primary input to ecosystems. Phosphorus is often the limiting nutrient in freshwater lakes and many terrestrial ecosystems; agricultural phosphate runoff causes eutrophication — algal blooms that deplete dissolved oxygen and kill fish through the resulting hypoxic dead zones. Global phosphate rock reserves (primarily Morocco's Western Sahara deposits) may limit agricultural productivity within 50–100 years, motivating phosphorus recovery from wastewater and manure.

The discovery of insulin by Frederick Banting and Charles Best in 1921 (Nobel Prize, Banting and Macleod, 1923) transformed type 1 diabetes from a fatal disease to a manageable condition. Modern insulins are recombinant human proteins produced in E. coli or yeast; engineered analogs with altered amino acid sequences produce rapid-acting (lispro, aspart: onset 15 min), intermediate, and long-acting (glargine: basal, 24h) pharmacokinetic profiles. Closed-loop insulin delivery ('artificial pancreas') systems combining CGM and algorithm-controlled pumps now achieve near-normal glycemic control in clinical use.

Sympatric sex determination systems include: gonochorism (most vertebrates — determined at fertilization by sex chromosomes XY or ZW), sequential hermaphroditism (changing sex during life — protandry, male first, in clownfish; protogyny, female first, in wrasse), and environmental sex determination (ESD, in many reptiles — temperature-dependent sex determination in turtles, where nest temperature during a critical developmental window determines sex). Crocodilians have TSD with a pivotal temperature range of ~1°C separating all-female from all-male offspring — highlighting vulnerability to climate warming.

source.name: Annual Review of Ecology and Systematics

text: Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) is a cofactor for prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases that hydroxylate proline and lysine residues in collagen chains, enabling the characteristic triple-helix structure of mature collagen. Without vitamin C, collagen cannot form properly, resulting in scurvy — the connective tissue disease that killed tens of thousands of sailors before James Lind's 1747 controlled trial showed citrus fruit prevented it. Vitamin C is also a major antioxidant in plasma and a cofactor for dopamine beta-hydroxylase (catecholamine synthesis) and carnitine biosynthesis.

Lichens form some of the primary colonizers of bare rock in polar, alpine, and post-volcanic environments. Crustose lichens physically penetrate rock surfaces by producing oxalic acid that weathers mineral surfaces; carbonic acid from lichen respiration further dissolves rock minerals. Over centuries, lichens create the organic matter and mineral particles that form the foundation of soil, supporting subsequent plant colonization — demonstrating a primary succession process that requires no pre-existing organic soil. Antarctic cryptoendolithic lichens grow inside translucent rocks, protected from UV and desiccation.

Neonicotinoids — systemic insecticides absorbed by plant tissues and expressed in pollen and nectar — have been extensively linked to bee colony collapse disorder (CCD) and population declines in pollinators. Sublethal neonicotinoid exposure impairs honeybee navigation (returning to the hive), disrupts memory, reduces foraging efficiency, and suppresses immune function increasing pathogen susceptibility. Large-scale field studies showed >50% decline in wild bee density in neonicotinoid-treated oilseed rape fields; the EU banned outdoor use of three neonicotinoids (clothianidin, imidacloprid, thiamethoxam) in 2018.

Human color vision derives from three types of cone photoreceptors (S, M, L) in the retina, with peak sensitivities at ~420, 530, and 560 nm respectively (absorbing short/blue, medium/green, and long/red wavelengths). Color is perceived from the ratio of signals across cone types: opponent processes in retinal ganglion cells encode red-green and blue-yellow contrasts before transmitting to visual cortex. Red-green color blindness (affecting ~8% of males) results from X-linked mutations deleting or merging M and L opsin genes; females with an extra cone type (tetrachromacy) may distinguish ~100 million colors versus the typical ~1 million.

source.name: Proceedings of the Royal Society B

text: The blood-brain barrier (BBB) is formed by tight junctions between brain capillary endothelial cells, astrocyte endfeet, and pericytes, creating a highly selective barrier that prevents most molecules >400 Da and most charged molecules from entering the brain while actively transporting nutrients (glucose via GLUT1, amino acids) and excluding neurotoxins. The BBB is both the brain's protection and the major obstacle to CNS drug delivery: 98% of small-molecule drugs and essentially all biologics cannot cross it. Strategies to overcome the BBB include focused ultrasound with microbubbles, nanoparticle carriers, and receptor-mediated transcytosis.

Cooperative hunting has independently evolved in several unrelated predator lineages. Harris's hawks (Parabuteo unicinctus) coordinate group hunts with role differentiation (flushing, ambushing prey); chimpanzees hunt colobus monkeys in coordinated groups with division of labor; bottlenose dolphins use mud-ring encirclement and strand feeding; army ants (Eciton burchellii) coordinate hundreds of thousands of individual ants via pheromone trails into a distributed collective hunting system that overwhelms prey far larger than any individual. Cooperative hunting typically increases prey size captured and individual feeding rates.

The plant hormone ethylene (C2H4), a gaseous molecule, regulates fruit ripening, leaf and petal abscission, flower development, and responses to stress and pathogens. Ethylene synthesis from methionine via ACC (1-aminocyclopropane-1-carboxylate) is stimulated by mechanical damage, drought, flooding, and pathogen attack. Ethylene receptors (ETR1 family) in the ER membrane are active in the absence of ethylene, repressing downstream signaling; ethylene binding inactivates the receptor and de-represses EIN3/EIL1 transcription factors activating ethylene response genes. Commercial fruit storage uses ethylene inhibitor 1-MCP to extend shelf life.

Deep-sea hydrothermal vent communities, first discovered at the Galapagos Rift in 1977, support dense ecosystems based on chemosynthesis rather than photosynthesis: bacteria and archaea oxidize hydrogen sulfide and methane from vent fluid to fix CO2 into organic carbon. Tubeworms (Riftia pachyptila) up to 2.4 m long harbor these chemosynthetic bacteria in a specialized trophosome organ comprising >50% of body mass, lacking a mouth or digestive tract and absorbing vent chemicals through plume tentacles. Cold seep communities on continental margins are similarly chemosynthesis-based but powered by methane seeping from seafloor sediments.

The thyroid gland produces thyroid hormones (T3 and T4) from iodination of thyroglobulin protein, regulated by hypothalamic TRH and pituitary TSH through a classic negative feedback loop. Thyroid hormones increase the metabolic rate of nearly all tissues by increasing mitochondrial number, uncoupling protein expression, and Na+/K+-ATPase activity — essential for thermogenesis, growth, and development. Congenital hypothyroidism (insufficient T3/T4) causes cretinism (severe intellectual disability) if untreated; universal newborn screening with blood spot TSH measurement and early T4 replacement prevents this entirely preventable condition.

The vertebrate jaw evolved from the branchial arches (gill supports) of jawless ancestors (agnathans); the first gill arch became the upper and lower jaw cartilages (Meckel's cartilage, palatoquadrate), while the second gill arch (hyoid) became the jaw suspension apparatus in fish. The mammalian ear evolved from jaw bones: the articular and quadrate bones (reptilian jaw joint) became the malleus and incus of the middle ear ossicles — one of the best-documented evolutionary transformations in the fossil record, supported by transitional fossils in Morganucodon and Adelobasileus.

source.name: Annual Review of Ecology and Systematics

text: Lipid metabolism begins with dietary triacylglycerols emulsified by bile salts and hydrolyzed by pancreatic lipase in the small intestine; free fatty acids and monoacylglycerols are absorbed by enterocytes, re-esterified into triacylglycerols, packaged into chylomicrons, and secreted into lymphatic lacteals, bypassing portal circulation. In the liver, very-low-density lipoproteins (VLDL) carry triglycerides to tissues; hydrolysis by lipoprotein lipase converts VLDL→IDL→LDL. LDL delivers cholesterol to cells via receptor-mediated endocytosis; excess LDL oxidation in arterial walls triggers atherosclerotic plaques. Statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, reducing hepatic cholesterol synthesis and upregulating LDL receptors.

Genomic structural variation — including copy number variants (CNVs, duplications/deletions >1 kb), inversions, translocations, and mobile element insertions — affects more base pairs of the human genome per individual than single nucleotide polymorphisms. CNVs contribute disproportionately to phenotypic variation, including large-effect CNVs at 16p11.2, 22q11.2, and 15q13.3 conferring substantial autism spectrum disorder and schizophrenia risk. The 22q11.2 deletion syndrome (DiGeorge/velocardiofacial syndrome, ~1/4,000 births) is the most common chromosomal microdeletion syndrome, causing heart defects, immunodeficiency, and psychiatric disorders.

Ant colonies exhibit sophisticated collective intelligence without any individual having a global view. Argentine ants (Linepithema humile) form the largest supercolony ever recorded — a single genetically related colony spanning 6,000 km across Southern Europe with billions of workers — because genetic similarity reduces intracolony aggression. Leafcutter ants (Atta species) maintain fungal gardens (monocultures of Leucoagaricus gongylophorus) as their sole food source, applying antibiotic-producing Streptomyces bacteria on their cuticle to control fungal pathogens of the garden — an agricultural mutualism preceding human farming by ~50 million years.

The evolution of multicellularity from unicellular ancestors has occurred independently at least 25 times (in animals, fungi, green algae, red algae, brown algae, slime molds, and multiple bacterial lineages). Multicellularity requires cells to remain associated after division, differentiate into specialized cell types, and cooperate rather than compete. Volvocine green algae (Chlamydomonas→Gonium→Eudorina→Volvox) form a graded series from unicellular to 2,000-cell organisms with germ-soma differentiation, providing an experimentally accessible model for studying how multicellularity evolves.

The avian lung's air sac system achieves crosscurrent gas exchange: air flows from the posterior air sacs through the parabronchi (the actual gas-exchange surface) and into the anterior air sacs before exiting — always in the same direction regardless of inspiration or expiration. Blood capillaries in the parabronchi flow in the opposite direction to airflow (countercurrent), maximizing the oxygen partial pressure gradient across the exchange surface. This system maintains near-constant blood oxygenation across the entire respiratory cycle, enabling high-altitude migration impossible for mammals with identical lung tidal breathing.

Pheromones are chemical signals secreted externally that trigger specific behavioral or physiological responses in other members of the same species. The Bombyx mori silk moth female pheromone bombykol (first identified in 1959 by Adolf Butenandt) can be detected by males at concentrations of a single molecule per milliliter of air, triggering upwind flight. Mammalian pheromones are detected by the vomeronasal organ (VNO) via V1R and V2R receptors distinct from olfactory receptors; humans have a vestigial VNO with mostly non-functional pheromone receptor genes, though behavioral evidence for human pheromone effects is debated.

The MAPK (mitogen-activated protein kinase) cascade is a ubiquitous signal transduction module: growth factor binding to RTKs activates Ras GTPase, which activates Raf kinase, which phosphorylates and activates MEK, which phosphorylates and activates ERK. ERK translocates to the nucleus and phosphorylates transcription factors controlling cell growth, differentiation, and survival. KRAS is the most commonly mutated oncogene in cancer (~25% of all cancers); BRAF V600E is the oncogenic driver in ~50% of melanomas, targeted by vemurafenib (BRAF inhibitor) and trametinib (MEK inhibitor) in combination.

Coral symbiodiniaceae (zooxanthellae) are dinoflagellate algae living inside coral cells in a tight mutualism: algae photosynthetically produce up to 90% of coral's carbon and energy needs; in return, coral provides CO2, inorganic nitrogen and phosphorus, and physical protection. Different Symbiodiniaceae clades (A–I) have different thermal tolerances; corals hosting thermotolerant Clade D Symbiodinium are more heat-resistant but grow more slowly. Genetic manipulation of Symbiodiniaceae to increase thermal tolerance is being explored as a way to engineer climate-resilient corals.

Organoid technology uses iPSCs or adult tissue stem cells to generate self-organizing three-dimensional mini-organs in vitro that recapitulate key structural and functional features of their in vivo counterparts. Intestinal organoids (initiated from single Lgr5+ adult intestinal stem cells) contain crypt-villus architecture with all intestinal cell types; brain organoids develop layered cortical structures with functional neurons; patient-derived tumor organoids preserve tumor genetic heterogeneity and are used to predict chemotherapy responses. Organoids bridge the gap between cell culture and animal models.

Virulence evolution in pathogens is shaped by the transmission-virulence trade-off: highly virulent strains that kill hosts quickly transmit less, selecting for intermediate virulence in pathogens with direct horizontal transmission. However, vector-borne pathogens (malaria, dengue) may evolve higher virulence since the vector transmits the pathogen before the host is too ill to be bitten; fecal-oral pathogens may evolve high virulence if incapacitation increases environmental shedding. Myxomatosis introduced to Australia evolved rapidly from very high to intermediate virulence as rabbit-adapted strains outcompeted highly lethal ones.

Coral reef structural complexity — the fractal texture of branching, massive, and tabular coral forms — provides habitat heterogeneity supporting diverse fish communities. Fish species richness on reefs scales with rugosity (surface complexity) because multiple microhabitat types support more specialized species. Reef structural complexity has declined ~40% globally since 1957 as coral bleaching and crown-of-thorns starfish outbreaks flatten reefs; projections suggest 90% loss of reef structure by 2100 under business-as-usual emissions, causing collapse of the fish communities supporting ~500 million people's protein supply.

Flow cytometry uses laser light to measure physical and fluorescent properties of thousands of individual cells per second as they pass through a focused laser beam in a fluid stream. Scattered light provides cell size (forward scatter) and granularity (side scatter); fluorescent antibodies conjugated to different dyes label specific surface or intracellular proteins. Mass cytometry (CyTOF) uses heavy metal isotope-labeled antibodies instead of fluorophores, enabling simultaneous measurement of >40 parameters per cell without spectral overlap. Flow cytometry is essential for immunophenotyping (CD4/CD8 T cell counting in HIV), cancer diagnosis (leukemia/lymphoma immunophenotyping), and research.

Insect metamorphosis takes two forms: holometabolous (complete metamorphosis: egg→larva→pupa→adult, in beetles, flies, moths, bees — 85% of insect species) and hemimetabolous (incomplete metamorphosis: egg→nymph→adult without pupal stage, in bugs, grasshoppers, dragonflies). During holometabolous pupal stage, larval tissues are largely histolysed (broken down by autophagy and phagocytosis) and rebuilt from imaginal discs — pre-specified groups of cells set aside in the larva. Juvenile hormone suppresses adult differentiation; its decline in final larval instars initiates metamorphosis.

Introns — non-coding sequences within eukaryotic genes that are spliced out of pre-mRNA — are found at high density in vertebrate genes (~8 introns per gene, averaging 3.4 kb each vs. ~60 bp exons). Introns are thought to have invaded early eukaryotic genes as Group II self-splicing elements, subsequently losing self-splicing ability and becoming dependent on the spliceosome. Introns have functional benefits: they enable alternative splicing (proteome expansion), they contain regulatory elements (enhancers in introns), and intron definition/exon definition mechanisms accelerate detection of new mutations affecting splicing.

Aposematism — conspicuous coloration (red, yellow, orange, black) warning predators of toxicity or unpalatability — is common in amphibians, insects, and marine invertebrates. Poison dart frogs (family Dendrobatidae) sequester arthropod-derived alkaloids (batrachotoxins, pumiliotoxins) in skin glands; frog coloration varies dramatically between populations and correlates with alkaloid diversity from local prey. Müllerian mimicry occurs when multiple unpalatable species converge on the same warning coloration (Heliconius butterflies), amplifying predator learning; Batesian mimicry involves palatable species mimicking toxic ones.

Neuromuscular disease can arise from mutations affecting any component of the motor unit: motor neuron soma (ALS — loss of upper and lower motor neurons; spinal muscular atrophy — loss of lower motor neurons from SMN1 mutations), the neuromuscular junction (myasthenia gravis — anti-AChR antibodies; Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome — anti-VGCC antibodies), the muscle fiber itself (muscular dystrophies — mutations in dystrophin and sarcoglycan complex structural proteins), or ion channel function (myotonia congenita — gain-of-function ClC-1 chloride channel mutations). Gene therapy with AAV-SMN1 (onasemnogene abeparvovec) for spinal muscular atrophy is curative when given pre-symptomatically.

The Burgess Shale (British Columbia, ~508 Ma) and Chengjiang biota (Yunnan, China, ~520 Ma) preserve exceptional soft-tissue fossils of Cambrian ocean organisms. Among the most enigmatic: Anomalocaris (1 m, apex predator with compound eyes and frontal grasping appendages — a 'great appendage' arthropod); Opabinia (5 compound eyes, proboscis with terminal claw); and Hallucigenia (bilateral rows of spines and tentacles, long debated which end was which). Recent phylogenetic analyses place most Cambrian 'weird wonders' as stem-group lineages of modern phyla rather than entirely extinct body plans.

Sex chromosomes in mammals evolved from an ancestral autosome pair that acquired a sex-determining gene (SRY in therian mammals); one chromosome (Y) then accumulated inversions suppressing recombination to keep male-benefit/female-detriment alleles linked to SRY. Non-recombining Y chromosome regions progressively accumulate deleterious mutations (Muller's ratchet) and lose genes; the human Y chromosome has degraded from ~1,500 ancestral genes to ~55 functional genes. Some rodents (voles, mole voles) have lost Y chromosomes entirely and use novel sex-determining genes; platypus has 10 sex chromosomes (5 X + 5 Y in males).

The protein kinase A (PKA) signaling pathway is activated when cAMP (produced by adenylate cyclase after Gs-GPCR activation) binds the regulatory subunits of PKA tetramers, releasing the active catalytic subunits. PKA phosphorylates glycogen phosphorylase kinase (activating glycogen breakdown), triglyceride lipase (fat mobilization), and CREB transcription factor (long-term gene expression changes). Cyclic nucleotide phosphodiesterases (PDEs) degrade cAMP, terminating the signal; PDE inhibitors (sildenafil/Viagra inhibiting PDE5) amplify cGMP signaling causing smooth muscle relaxation and vasodilation.

The firefly (Lampyridae) mating system uses species-specific bioluminescent flash patterns for mate signaling. Males fly and flash in species-specific rhythms; females on vegetation respond with a precisely timed flash. Photinus pyralis males flash once every 5.5 seconds, females reply after 2.1 seconds; species differ in flash interval, duration, and color. Femme fatale Photuris females mimic the reply flashes of Photinus females to lure Photinus males for predation — and then sequester the males' lucibufagins (defensive steroidal pyrones) for their own chemical defense against spider predation.

The replication of circular bacterial chromosomes initiates at a single origin (oriC) where DnaA proteins bind and recruit the DnaB helicase to unwind the DNA double helix; bidirectional replication forks proceed around the chromosome meeting at a terminus region. Chromosome condensation and segregation in bacteria are mediated by SMC (structural maintenance of chromosomes) complexes and ParABS systems that actively partition chromosome copies to cell poles before division. The FtsZ protein (tubulin homolog) forms the contractile Z-ring marking the division plane — the prokaryotic functional equivalent of the eukaryotic contractile ring.

The SARS-CoV-2 spike protein binds ACE2 (angiotensin-converting enzyme 2) on human cells with ~10–100 times higher affinity than SARS-CoV-1 spike; furin cleavage at the S1/S2 boundary enables efficient membrane fusion. ACE2 is highly expressed in type II pneumocytes, upper respiratory epithelium, intestinal enterocytes, heart, kidney, and olfactory neurons — explaining COVID-19's multiorgan manifestations including respiratory failure, cardiac injury, kidney injury, and anosmia. Omicron BA.2+ subvariants show reduced lung cell fusogenic capacity but increased upper respiratory tract replication, contributing to altered disease severity and transmissibility.

Population viability analysis (PVA) uses demographic data (birth rate, death rate, age structure) and stochastic modeling to estimate extinction probability over a given time horizon. The minimum viable population (MVP) concept specifies the smallest population size maintaining >95% probability of persistence for 100 years; typical MVP estimates range from 50–100 individuals (genetic concerns — 50/500 rule) to 1,000–10,000 individuals for long-lived species with environmental stochasticity. PVA is used to inform recovery targets for endangered species management and evaluate effectiveness of conservation interventions.

Phosphorus limitation shapes marine phytoplankton community structure in subtropical ocean gyres; phosphorus recycling is performed by alkaline phosphatase enzymes produced by bacteria and phytoplankton to acquire phosphate from organic compounds. Iron limitation constrains primary production in the Southern Ocean, equatorial Pacific, and subarctic Pacific — regions with abundant macronutrients (nitrate, phosphate) but low dissolved iron from distant dust sources (HNLC regions: high nutrient, low chlorophyll). Iron fertilization experiments demonstrated that iron addition triggers phytoplankton blooms in HNLC regions, providing proof-of-concept for carbon sequestration geoengineering.

Tetrodotoxin (TTX) is a potent neurotoxin produced by symbiotic bacteria (Pseudoalteromonas, Vibrio) in puffer fish (Tetraodontidae), blue-ringed octopuses, rough-skinned newts (Taricha granulosa), and some flatworms; puffer fish liver and ovaries accumulate TTX to concentrations causing death in humans within hours. TTX blocks voltage-gated sodium channels (Nav1.1–1.7) by occluding the channel pore from outside with sub-nanomolar affinity, preventing nerve and muscle action potentials. Rough-skinned newts produce enough TTX in single individuals to kill 25,000 mice; local garter snake populations (Thamnophis sirtalis) have evolved TTX-resistant Nav1.4 mutations in a coevolutionary arms race.

The Ediacaran biota (~575–539 Ma) — the oldest assemblage of macroscopic fossils — consisted primarily of soft-bodied organisms with quilted or frond-like body plans that do not clearly correspond to any modern animal phylum. Dickinsonia (up to 1.4 m), Charnia, and Rangea are iconic forms; their classification as animals, fungi, lichen, or an entirely extinct kingdom remains debated. Lipid biomarkers in Dickinsonia fossils include cholesterol-like compounds supporting animal affinity. The Ediacaran fauna mostly disappeared at the beginning of the Cambrian, potentially outcompeted by the newly evolving bilaterian animals.

Adaptive immunity evolves with the organism: lampreys and hagfish (jawless vertebrates) have convergently evolved an adaptive immune system based on variable lymphocyte receptors (VLRs) assembled from leucine-rich repeat modules — completely different from the immunoglobulin-based receptors of jawed vertebrates (gnathostomes). Jawed vertebrate RAG1/RAG2 recombinase mediates V(D)J recombination of immunoglobulin and TCR genes; RAG1/RAG2 are evolutionarily related to Transib DNA transposons, suggesting RAG-based immunity arose from transposon domestication ~500 million years ago.

Collagen is the most abundant protein in the human body (~30% of total protein mass), forming the structural scaffold of skin, bone, tendon, cartilage, and blood vessel walls. The three alpha-chains of collagen wind into a characteristic right-handed triple helix stabilized by repeated Gly-X-Y motifs (X=proline, Y=hydroxyproline); every third residue must be glycine (the smallest amino acid) to fit inside the triple helix. Mutations disrupting the Gly-X-Y repeat cause osteogenesis imperfecta (brittle bone disease); Ehlers-Danlos syndrome results from mutations in collagen biosynthesis enzymes or structural proteins.

Plant carnivory has evolved independently ~12 times in unrelated lineages (Droseraceae, Sarraceniaceae, Nepenthaceae, Lentibulariaceae, others) in response to nutrient-poor environments (bogs, fens, wet rock faces). The Venus flytrap and waterwheel plant (Aldrovanda) have homologous fast-moving snap-traps; pitcher plants (Nepenthes, Sarracenia, Cephalotus) have convergently evolved pitfall traps; bladderworts (Utricularia) use the most sophisticated trap — underwater suction bladders that create negative internal pressure and capture prey in 10 milliseconds by opening a trapdoor, the fastest plant movement known.

Cortisol (a glucocorticoid) is released from the adrenal cortex in response to ACTH from the pituitary, which is released in response to hypothalamic CRH — the classic HPA axis. Cortisol mobilizes glucose (stimulating gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis), suppresses immune responses (inhibiting NF-kB and reducing inflammatory cytokine production), and promotes fat and protein catabolism. Chronic stress and chronic cortisol elevation cause immunosuppression, hippocampal dendritic atrophy (impairing memory), and increased susceptibility to infection, cardiovascular disease, and type 2 diabetes.

The major histocompatibility complex (MHC) is the most polymorphic region of the vertebrate genome: human HLA (human leukocyte antigen) class I and II genes have thousands of alleles at multiple loci. This extreme polymorphism reflects balancing selection: heterozygosity confers advantage in pathogen defense (each allele presents different peptides), and mate choice for MHC dissimilarity (detected via olfactory cues) promotes outbreeding. Low MHC diversity in cheetahs and Florida panthers impairs immune function; MHC matching between donor and recipient is essential for organ transplant success.

Hibernation in mammals involves prolonged torpor with suppressed metabolic rate, heart rate, body temperature, and ventilation to conserve energy during winter when food is scarce. Arctic ground squirrels (Urocitellus parryii) reduce body temperature to -3°C — the lowest recorded for any hibernating mammal — using specific brain thermosensor mechanisms; black bears reduce metabolic rate by ~75% without entering deep torpor; the fat-tailed dwarf lemur (Cheirogaleus medius) hibernates up to 7 months storing fat in its tail. Understanding hibernation mechanisms inspires research on surgical hypothermia, stroke neuroprotection, and long-duration spaceflight.

Genome-wide chromatin conformation is captured by Hi-C technology, which crosslinks physically interacting chromatin loci, digests DNA, ligates proximal ends, and identifies contact pairs by paired-end sequencing. Hi-C maps reveal that chromosomes are organized into topologically associating domains (TADs) — self-interacting ~1 Mb regions — separated by boundaries enriched for CTCF protein and cohesin complexes. TAD boundaries insulate enhancers from promoters in adjacent TADs; boundary deletions cause ectopic enhancer-promoter contacts activating developmental genes in wrong tissues, causing congenital limb malformations and cancer.

The poison dart frog (Dendrobates tinctorius) is a textbook example of aposematism and co-evolutionary dynamics: wild frogs are toxic due to sequestered dietary mites and ants; captive-raised frogs eating non-toxic prey are non-toxic. The same alkaloids that make these frogs unpalatable also protect against bat ectoparasites — a secondary benefit. Strawberry poison frog (Oophaga pumilio) populations across the Bocas del Toro archipelago vary dramatically in color pattern (red, blue, green, yellow, orange) isolated on different islands, providing a model for studying the genetics and ecology of aposematic signal divergence and speciation.

TRPV1 (transient receptor potential vanilloid 1) is a calcium-permeable ion channel acting as a polymodal nociceptor activated by heat >43°C, capsaicin (the active compound in chili peppers), protons (low pH), endocannabinoids, and lipids. David Julius won the 2021 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for identifying TRPV1 through a strategy of expressing a human sensory neuron cDNA library in non-neuronal cells and screening for capsaicin responsiveness. TRPV1 antagonists (AMG-517, SB-705498) have been investigated as analgesics but cause hyperthermia side effects by blocking normal thermosensation.

The monarch butterfly population overwinters in oyamel fir (Abies religiosa) forests in the Sierra Madre mountains of Michoacán, Mexico, clustering on trees in densities of up to 4 million individuals per hectare. These trees provide a critical microclimate: the dense canopy insulates against freezing temperatures (monarchs can tolerate -4°C briefly but die at lower temperatures) while preventing overheating on warm winter days. The 2002 winter storm killed ~200 million monarchs (7–8% of the population) in a single event. Logging of oyamel habitat (legal and illegal) and milkweed loss on migration routes are primary threats to eastern monarch populations, which have declined >80% since the 1990s.

Long-read DNA sequencing technologies (Pacific Biosciences SMRT sequencing, Oxford Nanopore) generate reads >10 kb (sometimes >1 Mb), enabling de novo assembly of chromosomes, resolution of repetitive regions missed by short-read sequencing, and direct detection of DNA methylation from signal kinetics. The first truly complete human reference genome (T2T-CHM13, 2022) was assembled using long-read sequencing, adding 200 Mb of previously missing sequence including all centromeres, telomeres, and segmental duplications, revealing thousands of new genes and functional elements absent from the previous GRCh38 reference.

Evolutionary developmental biology has revealed that left-right body asymmetry in vertebrates is established during early embryogenesis at a specialized structure called the node (in mammals) or Hensen's node, where rotating monocilia generate a leftward fluid flow. This nodal flow activates calcium signaling and Nodal (a TGF-beta family member) expression specifically on the left side, triggering Lefty1, Lefty2, and Pitx2 transcription factors that specify left-side organ identity (heart looping, gut rotation, spleen position). Primary ciliary dyskinesia (PCD) from ciliary gene mutations causes random left-right determination (situs inversus or situs ambiguus) in ~50% of cases.

Marine mammals evolved from terrestrial ancestors multiple times: cetaceans (whales, dolphins) from Artiodactyla ~50 Ma; pinnipeds (seals, sea lions, walruses) from mustelid-like carnivores ~30 Ma; sirenians (manatees, dugongs) from a paenungulate ancestor ~55 Ma; and sea otters from mustelid ancestors ~3 Ma. All marine mammal lineages evolved improved swimming, dense bones for buoyancy control or ballast, increased fat (blubber) for insulation and energy storage, and physiological adaptations for breath-hold diving (elevated myoglobin, splenic erythrocyte reservoir, bradycardia diving reflex). These are striking examples of convergent evolution of marine adaptations.

source.name: Annual Review of Ecology and Systematics

text: Autophagy receptors (p62/SQSTM1, NDP52, optineurin, NBR1) link ubiquitin-tagged cargo to the autophagy machinery by binding both ubiquitin and LC3/GABARAP proteins on autophagosome membranes. Selective autophagy subtypes include mitophagy (damaged mitochondria via PINK1-Parkin pathway), xenophagy (intracellular bacteria tagged with ubiquitin), aggrephagy (protein aggregates), and lipophagy (lipid droplets via ATGL). PINK1 mutations cause early-onset Parkinson's disease; failure of mitophagy allows accumulation of dysfunctional mitochondria producing excess ROS, contributing to dopaminergic neuron death. Mitophagy enhancers are being explored therapeutically.

Diatom frustule silicification uses species-specific protein templates (silaffins, cingulins) to direct SiO2 deposition into intricate nano-patterns within specialized silica deposition vesicles (SDVs). These patterns can have submicron periodicity that diffracts light, producing iridescent structural colors in some species. The frustule's silica shell provides mechanical protection (resisting copepod mandible forces of 10–50 μN) while remaining optically clear to permit photosynthesis within; some diatom frustules transmit light via waveguide effects that concentrate light onto chloroplasts. These properties make diatom frustules attractive templates for nanotech applications.

Neurotrophins — small secreted proteins including NGF, BDNF, NT-3, NT-4 — promote survival, differentiation, and maintenance of neurons by binding Trk receptor tyrosine kinases (TrkA for NGF, TrkB for BDNF, TrkC for NT-3). The neurotrophic hypothesis proposes that neurons compete for limited target-derived neurotrophins and those receiving insufficient support undergo apoptosis — the mechanism explaining the ~50% programmed neuron death that normally occurs during nervous system development. Reduced BDNF signaling is linked to depression and neurodegenerative diseases; antidepressants increase hippocampal BDNF expression; TrkB agonists are being developed for neurological disorders.

Developmental gene regulatory networks (dGRNs) are hierarchical circuits of transcription factors and signaling molecules that control spatial and temporal gene expression during embryonic development. The sea urchin endomesoderm GRN — the most completely worked out dGRN — maps the precise gene regulatory interactions specifying the fate of every embryonic cell. GRNs exhibit robustness through redundant regulatory inputs (shadow enhancers) and feedback loops that canalize development against genetic and environmental perturbation. Eric Davidson pioneered dGRN analysis and proposed that dGRN evolution underlies body plan evolution.

Plasmids are extrachromosomal circular DNA molecules in bacteria that replicate independently and often carry adaptive genes (antibiotic resistance, virulence factors, metabolic capabilities). Conjugative plasmids encode a type IV secretion system (pilus + mating pair formation) enabling plasmid transfer to recipient bacteria in direct cell-cell contact. High-frequency conjugation of resistance plasmids (especially broad-host-range IncP plasmids) between clinical Enterobacteriaceae is a major driver of multi-drug resistance spread in healthcare settings. Bacteriophages also mediate resistance gene transfer via transduction.

The hummingbird hawk-moth (Macroglossum stellatarum) is one of the most remarkable examples of convergent evolution: this moth has evolved to hover in front of flowers and feed on nectar through a long proboscis in the same manner as hummingbirds, despite being separated by ~100 million years of evolution. It independently evolved excellent color vision, high wing-beat frequency (70–90 Hz, audible as a hum), hovering flight through wing-stroke adjustment, and compound eye optical flow processing for visual stabilization during hover. It even makes a humming sound — audible to human ears — from wing beats.

Synthetic biology engineers new biological systems by applying engineering principles to biology: standardized genetic 'parts' (promoters, ribosome-binding sites, coding sequences, terminators) are assembled into genetic 'devices' (genetic switches, oscillators, logic gates) and 'systems'. The first synthetic genetic oscillator (Elowitz and Leibler, 2000) used a three-repressor negative feedback loop in E. coli to generate periodic GFP oscillations. Synthetic gene circuits control CAR-T cell activity in cancer, produce antimalarial drug precursor artemisinic acid in yeast (scaling artemisinin production), and design live biotherapeutics for gut microbiome modulation.

Skeletal muscle contraction occurs via the sliding filament mechanism: myosin heads on thick filaments bind actin in thin filaments, perform a power stroke (rotating 45°→90°), and release in a cycle powered by ATP hydrolysis. Troponin-tropomyosin complexes on actin filaments block myosin-binding sites at rest; Ca2+ binding to troponin C shifts tropomyosin to expose myosin-binding sites, initiating contraction. The maximum force a muscle generates depends on sarcomere length (length-tension relationship) — optimal at the resting sarcomere length where maximal actin-myosin overlap occurs (~2.2 μm per sarcomere).

The woodpecker finch (Camarhynchus pallidus) of the Galapagos uses cactus spines and twigs to probe for insects in tree bark — one of the few avian tool uses. Darwin's finches (family Thraupidae, 18 species) evolved from a single South American seed-eating ancestor ~2–3 million years ago, diversifying in beak morphology to exploit different food sources (seeds, cacti, insects, blood). Peter and Rosemary Grant's 40-year study documented natural selection on beak size during drought years, providing one of the clearest real-time observations of evolution in wild populations.

White-nose syndrome (WNS), caused by the fungus Pseudogymnoascus destructans (Pd), has killed >6 million North American bats since its detection in 2006 and threatens the extinction of the little brown bat (Myotis lucifugus) within decades in its eastern range. Pd grows on bat skin during winter torpor, causing wing damage and aberrant arousal bouts that deplete fat reserves. European bats (where Pd likely originated) show resistance through different immune and behavioral responses. Biological control using Pseudomonas fluorescens bacteria that produce volatile antifungal compounds applied to cave walls significantly reduces Pd load in field trials.

source.name: Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B

text: ATP synthesis by the mitochondrial ATP synthase (Complex V, F0F1-ATPase) is driven by proton motive force: proton flow through the membrane-embedded F0 rotor (10–15 c-subunit ring) drives rotation of the central stalk, inducing conformational changes in the three beta-subunits of the F1 head that sequentially bind ADP+Pi, form ATP, and release ATP (rotary catalysis). Paul Boyer and John Walker received the 1997 Nobel Prize for elucidating this rotary mechanism; each 360° rotation produces 3 ATP; the mitochondrial ATP synthase can synthesize ~100 ATP/second at physiological proton gradients.

Somatic evolution in cancer parallels organismal evolution: cancer cells undergo mutation, selection, and clonal expansion. Multi-region tumor sequencing reveals extensive intratumor heterogeneity — different parts of the same tumor carry different mutations in a 'Darwinian' branching evolution. Liquid biopsy ctDNA tracking in breast cancer shows that metastatic clones diverge from primary tumors decades before metastasis is clinically detectable. Cancer cell populations engage in ecological competition (dominant clones suppressing subclones via resource depletion), cooperation (metabolic mutualism between neighboring clones), and phenotypic plasticity — concepts from ecology applied to tumor biology.

The RNA polymerase II (Pol II) transcription cycle involves a choreographed sequence of events: PIC (pre-initiation complex) assembly at promoters containing TATA box or BRE elements with general transcription factors (TFIID, TFIIB, TFIIH), promoter escape, pausing at +20–60 nt (controlled by NELF and DSIF), elongation activation by P-TEFb (CDK9/cyclin T) phosphorylating Pol II CTD Ser2, and termination coupled to mRNA 3' end cleavage/polyadenylation. Pol II CTD has 52 heptapeptide repeats (YSPTSPS) that serve as a platform for coordinating capping, splicing, polyadenylation, and export factors with transcription.

The marine iguana (Amblyrhynchus cristatus) of the Galapagos Islands is the world's only sea-going lizard, diving to depths of 15 m and feeding exclusively on algae scraped from rocks with specialized blunt snouts and laterally flattened tails for swimming. They face the thermal challenge of cooling rapidly in cold (15°C) Galapagos upwelling water; they bask on lava after diving to re-warm. During the 1997–98 El Niño, >70% of the population starved when warm water eliminated algae; survivors that shrank their body length (reabsorbing bone matrix to reduce metabolic needs) had higher survival — a reversible bone resorption unique among adult vertebrates.

Celiac disease is an autoimmune disorder in which gluten peptides (from wheat, barley, rye) are deamidated by tissue transglutaminase (TG2) and presented by HLA-DQ2 or HLA-DQ8 MHC class II molecules on APCs to gluten-reactive CD4+ T cells, triggering immune responses that damage intestinal villous enterocytes through CD8+ T cell-mediated killing and antibody-dependent mechanisms. The resulting villous atrophy impairs nutrient absorption, causing malabsorption, anemia, osteoporosis, and increased lymphoma risk. Celiac affects ~1% of the population; strict gluten-free diet is the only treatment.

The therapsid-to-mammal transition — documented over >100 million years of fossil record — is one of the most complete evolutionary sequences in vertebrate paleontology. Therapsids (synapsid reptiles) progressively acquired mammalian features: secondary palate enabling simultaneous breathing and chewing (Thrinaxodon), differentiated heterodont teeth (incisors, canines, molars), upright posture (Cynognathus), reduced quadrate-articular bones (later incorporated into middle ear), and eventually endothermy and hair (inferred from vibrissae pits in snout fossils). The Triassic Morganucodon is one of the earliest true mammals (~225 Ma).

Genome editing by CRISPR-Cas9 has been applied in human clinical trials for sickle cell disease and beta-thalassemia by reactivating fetal hemoglobin (HbF) expression in adult red blood cells. BCL11A, a transcriptional repressor of the fetal globin (gamma-globin) gene, is the target: disrupting BCL11A enhancer sequences in hematopoietic stem cells using Cas9 de-represses HbF to levels sufficient to compensate for defective adult hemoglobin. Casgevy (exagamglogene autotemcel) — the first CRISPR therapy approved (US/UK, 2023) — achieves functional cure in >90% of sickle cell patients treated.

Insect navigation is mediated by a specialized brain structure called the central complex — a set of neuropils (central body, protocerebral bridge, noduli) conserved across all insects that functions as a navigation center. Locust and dung beetle central complex neurons encode compass information from celestial cues (sun, moon, Milky Way polarization) and are mapped in a 360° ring attractor network. Monarch butterfly central complex neurons integrate time-compensated sun azimuth with a circadian clock to compute a fixed-direction vector used for fall southward migration across North America.

Oxygen-evolving photosynthesis requires a light-harvesting complex that captures photons and transfers excitation energy to the reaction center via Förster resonance energy transfer (FRET) in femtosecond timescales. The oxygen-evolving complex (OEC) in Photosystem II contains a Mn4CaO5 cluster that accumulates four oxidizing equivalents (S0→S1→S2→S3→S4) from successive charge separations before releasing O2 from two water molecules — the Kok cycle (S-state transitions). This elegant chemistry, achieving water oxidation at 0°C with ~70% quantum efficiency, inspires artificial photosynthesis research for solar fuel production.

De novo gene birth — the emergence of entirely new protein-coding genes from non-genic sequences — is now recognized as more common than previously thought. Orphan genes unique to one lineage (ORFan genes) arise when random mutations convert non-coding sequences into open reading frames with accessible chromatin, enabling transcription and translation. De novo genes are disproportionately expressed in testis and brain — tissues with relaxed transcriptional control — and may serve as raw material for evolutionary innovation. The antifreeze protein gene of the Antarctic notothenioid icefish arose de novo from non-coding repetitive DNA ~10 Ma.

The naked mole rat's genome encodes an unusual form of hyaluronic acid (HMW-HA) five times larger than that in most mammals, produced by a highly active HAS2 gene. HMW-HA fills the extracellular space in naked mole rat tissues and is thought to suppress cancer through contact inhibition and activation of p16 and p53 pathways when cell density rises. Early-contact inhibition (ECI) — a cell-density sensing mechanism unique to naked mole rats — triggers cell cycle arrest at much lower cell densities than other rodents. Experimentally degrading HMW-HA or removing ECI allows naked mole rat cells to form tumors.

Bacterial sporulation in Bacillus subtilis involves a cascade of sigma factor activation creating a developmental program in which a single vegetative cell produces a metabolically dormant endospore capable of surviving extreme heat (121°C for 30 minutes in some strains), UV radiation, desiccation, and chemical disinfection for decades to centuries. Endospore inner and outer coats contain dipicolinic acid chelating calcium, cross-linked spore coat proteins, and specialized DNA-binding proteins (SASPs) protecting DNA from damage. Anthrax (Bacillus anthracis) endospores persist in soil for decades and were weaponized as bioterrorism agents.

The concept of niche construction — organisms modifying their environments and thereby altering natural selection — extends the standard evolutionary framework. Beavers engineer wetland ecosystems through dam-building that creates ponds, alters hydrology, affects nutrient cycling, and changes local biodiversity; earthworms alter soil structure, pH, and microbial communities as they burrow and process organic matter; humans have so extensively modified global environments (the Anthropocene) that their niche-construction activities now dominate evolutionary pressures on thousands of species. Niche construction extends the Modern Synthesis by making ecology-evolution feedbacks central.

The complement system is a cascade of >30 proteins in blood and on cell surfaces that amplify innate immune responses to pathogens. Three pathways (classical, activated by antibody-antigen complexes; lectin, by carbohydrate patterns; alternative, by spontaneous hydrolysis of C3 on foreign surfaces) converge on C3 convertase, which cleaves C3 into C3b (opsonin coating bacteria for phagocytosis) and C3a (anaphylatoxin). Terminal complement cascade assembles the MAC (membrane attack complex, C5b-9) that perforates pathogen membranes. Hereditary angioedema results from C1-inhibitor deficiency causing uncontrolled bradykinin release; paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria from loss of GPI-anchored complement regulators (CD55, CD59) on red blood cells.

Chromosome segregation errors during meiosis (non-disjunction) produce aneuploid gametes; fertilization with aneuploid gametes causes chromosomal aneuploidy in the embryo. Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome, ~1/700 live births) arises from non-disjunction of chromosome 21 — risk increases dramatically with maternal age (from ~0.1% at age 25 to ~3% at age 40) because human oocytes arrest in prophase I for decades, with the cohesion holding homologous chromosomes together degrading progressively. Trisomies 13 (Patau) and 18 (Edwards) are usually fatal in infancy; monosomy X (Turner syndrome, 45,X) causes short stature and gonadal dysgenesis.

The chaperonin GroEL/GroES system (Hsp60/Hsp10 homologs) in E. coli forms a cylindrical protein folding cage: a misfolded protein is captured inside the GroEL barrel, GroES caps the opening, and iterative cycles of ATP-driven conformational changes provide a hydrophilic, confined environment promoting correct folding while preventing aggregation. ~250–300 E. coli proteins require GroEL for folding under normal conditions; at heat-shock temperatures, when many more proteins unfold, GroEL/GroES becomes essential for cell survival. The eukaryotic equivalent (TRiC/CCT complex) folds tubulin, actin, and ~10% of the newly synthesized eukaryotic proteome.

The wood frog (Rana sylvatica) survives winter by freezing solid — two-thirds of its body water forms ice crystals filling the abdominal and sub-skin spaces — and revives in spring as ice melts. Cryoprotection involves rapid glucose production from liver glycogen (concentrations >200 mM in plasma — 150× normal) that prevents intracellular ice formation; organs remain functional after thawing despite apparent death (no heartbeat, no breathing) during freezing. Understanding wood frog freeze tolerance inspires cryopreservation research for organ banking — enabling longer storage of transplant organs currently viable for only 4–24 hours.

Molecular clock dating uses rates of DNA sequence evolution to estimate divergence times between lineages. The strict molecular clock (constant rate across lineages) was proposed by Zuckerkandl and Pauling in 1965; relaxed molecular clock models (allowing rates to vary between branches) are now standard in Bayesian phylogenetics with fossil calibration points. Molecular clock analyses have estimated the divergence of humans and chimpanzees at 6–7 Ma, the last common ancestor of all modern humans at ~150,000–300,000 years ago (consistent with the African origin of Homo sapiens), and the divergence of early tetrapod lineages much earlier than the fossil record previously suggested.

source.name: Annual Review of Ecology and Systematics

text: The Giardia lamblia parasite, infecting ~280 million people worldwide with giardiasis (causing diarrhea and malabsorption), lacks mitochondria but possesses mitosomes — highly reduced organelles retaining only iron-sulfur cluster assembly. Giardia's two nuclei are not fused but replicate synchronously and divide at mitosis; it is a diplomonad, and its genome is one of the most streamlined eukaryotic genomes known (~11.7 Mb, minimal non-coding DNA). Giardia's VSP (variant-specific surface proteins) undergo antigenic variation during infection, enabling immune evasion and prolonged chronic infection.

The Cori cycle is an inter-organ metabolic pathway: skeletal muscle produces lactate during anaerobic exercise, which is transported to the liver where it is converted back to glucose via gluconeogenesis (requiring 6 ATP) and released into blood for re-use by muscle. This cycle costs 2 ATP net per lactate molecule recycled — a metabolic investment that allows muscle to maintain ATP production beyond aerobic capacity. The cycle was discovered by Carl and Gerty Cori, who shared the 1947 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine (Gerty Cori was the first woman to win the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine).

Antiporter proteins exchange one ion or molecule for another across a membrane. The Na+/H+ antiporter (NHE, SLC9 family) in the plasma membrane extrudes one H+ out of the cell (reducing cytoplasmic acidity) in exchange for one Na+ in, driven by the Na+ electrochemical gradient. Cancer cells upregulate NHE1, creating an alkaline intracellular pH that promotes proliferation and a paradoxically acidic extracellular microenvironment from accumulated protons — contributing to the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment. Mitochondrial Ca2+/Na+ antiporter (NCLX) regulates mitochondrial calcium homeostasis and is a potential heart failure therapeutic target.

Photoperiodism — the biological response to day length — governs seasonal timing of flowering, reproduction, migration, and hibernation. Short-day plants (chrysanthemum, poinsettia) flower when night length exceeds a critical threshold; long-day plants (Arabidopsis) flower when night length falls below threshold. The critical signal is the dark period, not day length: even brief light pulses during the long night (night break) can prevent flowering in short-day plants. Flowering time measurement involves circadian-clock-regulated CO (CONSTANS) protein that accumulates under long days and activates FT (FLORIGEN) in leaves, which travels to the shoot apical meristem to initiate flowering.

The IPEX syndrome (immune dysregulation, polyendocrinopathy, enteropathy, X-linked) results from mutations in FOXP3, the master transcription factor for regulatory T cell (Treg) identity and function. Without functional Tregs, mice and humans develop severe multi-organ autoimmunity at birth — validating Tregs as essential suppressors of self-reactive T cells. FOXP3 mutations affect ~1/1,600,000 male births and are uniformly fatal without bone marrow transplantation. The successful transfer of immune suppression from one individual to another by adoptive transfer of Tregs in IPEX mice established that Tregs suppress autoimmunity in a dominant, cell-extrinsic manner.

Sea turtles demonstrate natal homing: females return to the exact beach where they were hatched decades earlier to lay their own eggs, navigating across thousands of kilometers of open ocean. They use magnetic maps, detecting both the inclination angle and intensity of Earth's magnetic field to determine latitude and longitude — an ability demonstrated by exposing hatchlings to artificial magnetic fields corresponding to different ocean locations, which altered their swimming direction appropriately. Temperature of nest incubation determines sex ratio in sea turtles (warmer nests produce more females); climate warming is skewing populations toward >90% female on some beaches.

Replication protein A (RPA) is a heterotrimeric single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) binding protein that protects ssDNA at replication forks, damaged DNA, and recombination intermediates from degradation and secondary structure formation. RPA coordinates the repair pathway by recruiting specific repair factors: ATRIP (ATR kinase activator, triggering S-phase checkpoint), RAD51 recombinase (HR repair), and XPA (nucleotide excision repair). Replication stress — caused by oncogene activation, nucleotide depletion, or DNA structure barriers — exhausts RPA, collapsing replication forks and triggering genomic instability that is both a cancer driver and a vulnerability exploitable therapeutically.

Seasonal migration in birds is controlled by endocrine changes triggered by photoperiod: increasing day length in spring activates hypothalamic GnRH, stimulating gonadal development, and also triggers deposition of fat reserves (hyperphagia) and restlessness behavior (Zugunruhe). Geographic orientation during migration uses multiple compass systems: a sun compass (time-compensated), a magnetic compass (detecting Earth's field via cryptochrome-based radical pair mechanism in the eye or magnetite particles), and star compass (pattern of stellar rotation around Polaris learned during a critical developmental period). Birds also integrate olfactory cues and landmark memory for fine-scale navigation.

CRISPR-based diagnostics (SHERLOCK, DETECTR) use Cas13 (targeting RNA) or Cas12a (targeting DNA) enzymes with collateral cleavage activity: upon binding a target nucleic acid, activated Cas13 non-specifically degrades fluorescent reporter RNA in solution, producing a signal proportional to target concentration. Combined with isothermal amplification (LAMP, RPA), these assays detect pathogen nucleic acids with attomolar sensitivity and single-base-pair discrimination. During the COVID-19 pandemic, SHERLOCK-based SARS-CoV-2 tests were deployed in resource-limited settings due to their low cost, room-temperature stability, and lateral flow strip readout without laboratory equipment.

Mechanotransduction is the conversion of mechanical forces into biochemical signals in cells. Mechanosensing is critical for stem cell differentiation — mesenchymal stem cells on soft substrates (mimicking brain, ~0.5 kPa) differentiate into neurons; on intermediate stiffness (muscle, ~10 kPa) into myocytes; on hard substrates (bone, ~30 kPa+) into osteoblasts — mediated by actomyosin contractility and YAP/TAZ transcription co-activators. Cardiomyocytes in failing hearts experience abnormal mechanical stretch that activates hypertrophic signaling (calcineurin-NFAT pathway); anti-heart failure drugs partly target these mechanotransduction pathways.

The hagfish slime is one of the most unusual biomaterials in nature: a single gland secretes both mucin glycoproteins and protein threads (intermediate filament protein skeins) separately, which mix with seawater to form a gel exceeding 1 liter within seconds. The thread cells (skeins of 15 cm threads wound at 1 μm diameter) unravel in milliseconds upon contact with seawater — one of the fastest uncoiling events in biology. Engineering hagfish thread proteins in recombinant systems and bacteria has produced biomimetic fibers with mechanical properties rivaling Kevlar, with potential applications in biodegradable protective materials.

Pollinators perform an ecosystem service valued at $235–577 billion annually in global food production; ~75% of leading food crops worldwide depend at least partially on animal pollination (mainly bees, but also butterflies, moths, flies, beetles, birds, bats). Evidence from multiple continents documents declines in wild bee diversity and abundance driven by habitat loss, pesticide exposure, pathogens (Varroa mites + deformed wing virus in honeybees), and climate change. Wild bees are more effective per-visit pollinators than honeybees for many crops; loss of wild bee diversity reduces pollination stability under variable conditions.

Reactive astrocytes respond to CNS injury and disease by undergoing morphological and gene expression changes (astrogliosis) that produce a glial scar. Two distinct astrocyte reactive states exist: A1 astrocytes (induced by neuroinflammation via C3 secretion, promoting neurodegeneration) and A2 astrocytes (induced by ischemia, potentially neuroprotective). Astrocytes also regulate synapse formation, elimination, and function by secreting synaptogenic factors (thrombospondins, SPARC) and by controlling extracellular glutamate via GLT-1 transporter reuptake. Failure of GLT-1-mediated glutamate reuptake contributes to excitotoxic neuron death in ALS.

Sleep is a conserved biological process across all animals studied (including fruit flies, fish, and jellyfish) suggesting ancient evolutionary origin. During mammalian sleep, the brain cycles through non-REM (NREM, slow-wave sleep with delta oscillations reflecting cortical down-states) and REM (rapid eye movement, active cortex, dreaming, memory consolidation) stages. The glymphatic system — a paravascular CSF circulation driven by aquaporin-4 channels on astrocyte endfeet — is active mainly during NREM sleep, clearing metabolic waste including amyloid-beta at 10× daytime rates, potentially explaining why chronic sleep deprivation accelerates Alzheimer's pathology.

The poison of cone snails (family Conidae, ~800 species) contains conotoxins — small disulfide-rich peptides targeting ion channels and receptors with exquisite selectivity; individual species produce 50–200 different conotoxins, totaling an estimated 50,000–140,000 distinct peptides across the family. Conotoxin omega-MVIIA from Conus magus targeting N-type voltage-gated calcium channels was developed into ziconotide (Prialt), an intrathecal analgesic for severe chronic pain that is 1,000× more potent than morphine and non-addictive. Cone snail venom is thus a treasure trove of pharmacological tools and drug leads.

The epiblast of the early mammalian embryo undergoes a symmetry-breaking event called gastrulation: cells ingress through a thickening called the primitive streak to form the three primary germ layers — ectoderm (outer layer: skin, nervous system), mesoderm (middle: muscle, bone, heart, blood), and endoderm (inner: gut, lung, liver epithelium). BMP4 and Wnt3 signals from extraembryonic tissue initiate streak formation; Nodal-SMAD2/3 signaling drives mesendoderm specification; FGF8 and Snai1 drive epithelial-mesenchymal transition of ingressing epiblast cells. Human gastrulation (day 14–16 post-fertilization) is the basis for the '14-day rule' limiting human embryo research.

Dendritic cells (DCs) are specialized innate immune cells that sample antigens in peripheral tissues, process them into peptide fragments, and migrate to lymph nodes where they present antigen to naive T cells, initiating adaptive immune responses. Plasmacytoid DCs produce enormous quantities of type I interferons (IFN-alpha/beta) upon viral detection via TLR7/9, providing critical early antiviral innate defense. Ralph Steinman discovered dendritic cells in 1973 and received the 2011 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for their discovery, announced three days after his death from pancreatic cancer — the only Nobel awarded posthumously to a recently deceased laureate.

Spider silk is pound-for-pound stronger than steel (tensile strength ~1.5 GPa), more elastic than nylon, and tougher (energy to break) than Kevlar. Dragline silk from Nephila spiders consists of two proteins (MaSp1, MaSp2) with repetitive crystalline polyalanine blocks embedded in glycine-rich amorphous matrix; spinning through a pH gradient and water-recycling spigot converts disordered protein solution into aligned semicrystalline fiber. The orb weaver web combines different silk types: sticky capture spiral (viscid silk), non-sticky radii (dragline), and attachment points (tubuliform); commercial production of recombinant silk proteins is advancing for biomedical and materials applications.

Panspermia — the hypothesis that life can travel between planets on meteorites or comets — is supported by the discovery that viable bacteria, fungi, and cryptobiotic tardigrades can survive the harsh conditions of space (vacuum, radiation, temperature extremes) for short periods. Radiotolerant bacteria like Deinococcus radiodurans can endure 1.5 million rads of gamma radiation (2,000× lethal dose for humans) through massively redundant DNA repair mechanisms that reassemble shattered chromosomes within hours. Lithopanspermia (rock-mediated transfer) between Mars and Earth is plausible given meteorite exchange rates — ~100 kg of Mars material reaches Earth annually.

The PI3K-AKT-mTOR pathway is one of the most frequently activated oncogenic pathways in human cancer, downstream of multiple receptor tyrosine kinases and RAS. PI3K phosphorylates PIP2 to PIP3, recruiting AKT to the membrane for activation; AKT phosphorylates numerous substrates including mTORC1, GSK3, and FOXO transcription factors, promoting cell growth, survival, and metabolism. PTEN, a PIP3 phosphatase, acts as a major tumor suppressor — PTEN loss occurs in ~40% of glioblastomas. Everolimus and temsirolimus (mTORC1 inhibitors) are approved for renal cell carcinoma; combinations targeting PI3K and MEK are being evaluated to overcome resistance.

Sponges (phylum Porifera) are the most basal extant animals — they diverged before the evolution of symmetry, differentiated tissues, or a nervous system. Despite lacking neurons, sponges contract in waves through electrical signals propagated by calcium across a syncytial pinacoderm, suggesting that electrical excitability predates the nervous system. Choanocytes — flagellated cells lining sponge canals — create water currents filtering bacteria and particles from seawater; they are structurally identical to choanoflagellates, the closest living relatives of animals, linking animal multicellularity to flagellated unicellular ancestors.

Epigenetic reprogramming occurs at two key stages in mammalian development: during early embryogenesis (within ~24 hours of fertilization), when most parental DNA methylation is erased from the paternal genome by active demethylation via TET enzymes and from the maternal genome by passive replication-dependent dilution; and during primordial germ cell (PGC) specification, when imprints are also erased and later re-established sex-specifically during gametogenesis. This two-stage demethylation/re-methylation cycle resets the epigenome to totipotency and establishes parent-of-origin imprints in gametes.

Feathers are complex keratinized skin appendages unique to birds (and some non-avian dinosaurs), evolved from reptilian scales through a hierarchical follicular development program. Feather diversity is extreme: contour feathers provide aerodynamic shape, down feathers insulate (with interlocking barbule hooks disrupted by preening but re-zippered easily), and display feathers attract mates via structural color (peacock tail, hummingbird gorget) or iridescence. The dinosaur-to-bird feather transition is documented by exceptionally preserved fossils showing melanosomes allowing color reconstruction: Microraptor had iridescent black feathers; Sinosauropteryx had orange-brown and white banding.

The human genome's repeat sequences include short interspersed nuclear elements (SINEs, particularly Alu elements — ~300 bp primate-specific retrotransposons comprising ~11% of the genome with >1 million copies), long interspersed nuclear elements (LINEs, ~21%), and tandem repeats (centromeres, telomeres, microsatellites). Alu elements have contributed exon sequences, poly-A signal sequences, splice sites, and transcription factor binding sites to human genes; disease-causing Alu insertions and Alu-mediated deletion (non-allelic homologous recombination between nearby Alu copies) account for ~0.3% of new human genetic diseases.

Leaf architecture is precisely controlled during development: stomata (pores regulating CO2 uptake and water loss) are positioned by short-range peptide signaling to ensure no two stomata are adjacent (one-cell-spacing rule). Guard cells flanking each stoma change shape by swelling (opening) when K+ and water influx increases turgor, or shrinking (closing) when ABA hormone triggers K+ and anion efflux — a response triggered by drought, CO2 elevation, and darkness. Plants with elevated CO2 typically produce fewer stomata per unit leaf area, a phenomenon recorded in leaf cuticle fossils allowing past atmospheric CO2 estimation.

The spiny mouse (Acomys cahirinus) is unique among rodents in having regenerative wound healing: skin wounds heal without scarring through regeneration of hair follicles, dermis, and cartilage rather than fibrotic repair. This contrasts with most mammals where fibrosis is the dominant repair response. Spiny mice can also completely regenerate full-thickness ear pinnae punches including cartilage, epidermis, dermis, and hair follicles — abilities lost in other rodents. Comparative transcriptomics between healing spiny mouse and scarring laboratory mouse wounds revealed differences in TGF-beta3/TGF-beta1 ratios and macrophage polarization that may be manipulated to improve human wound healing.

The lac operon in E. coli is the classic model of gene regulation: three structural genes (lacZ encoding beta-galactosidase, lacY encoding lactose permease, lacA encoding transacetylase) are regulated by the lacI repressor protein, which binds the operator and blocks RNA polymerase when lactose is absent. Allolactose (a lactose metabolite) binds the repressor, causing conformational change and operator release, enabling transcription. A second level of regulation (catabolite repression) requires cAMP-CAP (catabolite activator protein) complex to bind an upstream site — only present at low glucose, ensuring lactose genes are only expressed when glucose is absent but lactose is present.

The gibbon family (Hylobatidae, 20 species) are the smallest and most acrobatic apes, using brachiation (swinging arm-over-arm through trees) as their primary locomotion — reaching speeds of 55 km/h and spanning 15 m gaps per swing. Gibbons have hyper-mobile ball-and-socket wrists that rotate 180° enabling under-branch swinging; enlarged curved fingers and reduced thumbs are specializations for branch grasping. They are the only apes to form pair bonds (with complex vocal duetting to maintain territory), though genetic studies reveal extra-pair paternity in ~11% of offspring. Their karyotypes show remarkable divergence from other apes (2n = 44, 50, or 52 depending on species) due to frequent chromosomal rearrangements.

RNA secondary structure — the intramolecular base pairing patterns of RNA molecules — profoundly influences RNA function. Riboswitches are structured RNA elements in bacterial mRNA 5' untranslated regions that bind specific metabolites (amino acids, vitamins, purines) and undergo conformational switches that control translation initiation or transcription termination. The SAM (S-adenosylmethionine) riboswitch family has >25,000 members across bacteria; thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP) riboswitches are found in eukaryotes as well, representing ancient regulatory mechanisms predating proteins. RNA G-quadruplex structures at mRNA 5' caps inhibit translation and are deregulated in cancer.

The origin of eukaryotes involved the endosymbiotic acquisition of both mitochondria (~1.8 Ga) and plastids (~1.5 Ga), but the archaeal host cell acquisition remains debated. The Asgard archaea — a superphylum discovered from deep-sea sediment metagenomes — encode many eukaryotic signature proteins (cytoskeletal actins, GTPases, ESCRT-III) previously thought unique to eukaryotes. Lokiarchaeota and related Asgard groups are inferred to be the closest archaeal relatives of eukaryotes; live cultures of Candidatus Asgardarchaeota have branched tentacle-like projections suggesting possible phagocytic capacity for capturing the bacterial mitochondrial ancestor.
